# International Scholarships and Fellowships
## Harkness Fellowships
Evolved from the Commonwealth Fund (est. 1918) into a dedicated program in 1961, Harkness Fellowships support international scholars in health care policy and practice. Now offering twelve-month research positions exclusively in health at top U.S. institutions, the program is funded by the Commonwealth Fund and international donors, featuring annual seminars and producing distinguished alumni from various countries.

# International Scholarships and Fellowships
## Studienstiftung des deutschen Volkes
Founded in 1925 and re-established in 1948, this foundation promotes excellence for students in Germany, the EU, and Switzerland. It awards scholarships at bachelor's, master's, and doctoral levels (PhDs receive €1,550–€1,750/month) based on BAFöG eligibility, offering tax-free payments, allowances, and access to research groups. The foundation awards approximately 2,480 scholarships annually (0.48% of German students), with notable alumni including multiple Nobel Prize winners in natural sciences, as well as leaders in social sciences, business, politics, arts, and journalism. University participation varies significantly, with Heidelberg University having the highest proportion (2.25%) and Bucerius Law School the highest absolute percentage (8.41%).

# International Scholarships and Fellowships
## Shuping Scholarship
Established in Shanghai in 1939 by industrialist Koo Soh Bing in memory of his father, this scholarship honors Koo's values of filial piety, honesty, and tolerance. Originally awarded between 1939–1949, the program was revived in 1986 with government support, expanding to over 6,000 recipients by 2000. Koo, who remained dedicated to the cause until his death in 1998, ensured its long-term sustainability through a 1995 donation of HK$10 million, a property in Shanghai, and the establishment of the Shuping Scholarship Foundation in Hong Kong and an Executive Committee in China. The scheme currently supports students at 37 secondary and 24 tertiary institutions across Shanghai, Beijing, and Huzhou, managed through voluntary Alumni Associations. Beyond monetary awards, the program emphasizes moral and physical education through extracurricular activities and has evolved over nearly 60 years to include student support systems (libraries, medical aid, vocational training), scholar associations, performing arts classes, and hardship awards. Historically, during its first decade, 1,100 recipients participated in initiatives such as a home for refugee children and an emergency medical fund, with many later becoming pivotal figures in China's modernization.
